utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber is a bit puzzled, Mr. Tieger, by the way the OTP is operating at this moment. There was a message last Friday just before 5.00 that what we should prepare to bring, of course what we did is to find the material and look at it and make sure that it would be there because it would save half a wood again. Then this morning, at five minutes past 9.00, where the Court were to start at 9.00, we got a message that it was all not -- no, I must say this was a -- we received it only at 9.00 but it was sent just before 3.00 this night. "Please disregard request last Friday for Judges' secretary to bring binders." Of course the work was done and we start 15 minutes late. It's not something that amuses the Chamber. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour -- well, first of all it's not something that pleases the Prosecution either, and I'm sorry for the Court's trouble. I hope it's clear at a minimum that we were on the same -- operating under the same principle, which was the desire to save labour and paper. That's what we attempted to signal. Unfortunately, in the process of communicating that, there was a misunderstanding and those documents were indeed printed out. Once that happened, and I take responsibility for that error, then it seemed that there was no purpose in having those documents in court in full and having the Court as well drag them down here. Apparently it didn't save the Court any time, but under the circumstances, it was best at least to let the Court know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I do agree that it's that it's best to let the Court know but let's not spend more time on it. It's -- are you ready to call your next witness, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution's next witness is Mr. Milan Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Usher, will you please escort Mr. Trbojevic into the courtroom. I never know where the accent is, is it Trbojevic or Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have the same question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could carefully listen to the witness and find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Cmeric always says Trbojevic and I don't very often argue with her about the pronunciation of Serbian names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I put the question mainly because Mr. Tieger said Mr. Trbojevic and I had Trbojevic in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness enters, I might note that he comes here under the same circumstances essentially as witnesses we've dealt with earlier for whom the Court gave warnings. I don't have any additional information to offer beyond that but I make that observation to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Looking at the way he was interviewed, what was said to him then, of course, was a bit different because he was not under any obligation to answer. Here he is, unless he -- I'll take care of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trbojevic. Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher will hand out to you the text of this declaration. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Trbojevic. Mr. Trbojevic, before your examination will start, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that you may object to answer any question which -- to which the answer might tend to incriminate yourself. Under those circumstances, we can compel you to answer that question, but if you are compelled this way to answer that question, your answer cannot be used as evidence in any subsequent prosecution against yourself for any offence other than false testimony. I take it that you understand this since I learned that you're a trained lawyer, so I take it that you understand the importance of this rule.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We haven't met, sir. My name is Alan Tieger and I represent the Office of the Prosecution. I'd like to begin today by providing the Court with some general idea of your background and professional qualifications and political experience. First of all, sir, I understand that you attended secondary school and graduated from the Gimnazija in Jajce in 1962; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, I see that you have -- I can't see what the papers are - they may well be empty - but whenever you think it would be necessary -- it's empty or is it ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just sheets of paper, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine, I couldn't see that from here, but you're not, without permission of the Court, you're not allowed to consult any papers, as you'll understand. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thereafter, sir, I understand that you graduated from the faculty of law in Sarajevo in 1966; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that you served as a judge in Sarajevo until -- from 1997 [sic], beginning in the primary court and then moving up to the district court where you served until October of 1990; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was a judge from the beginning of 1977 until the end of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that capacity, you worked in both the primary and subsequently the district court; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in October of 1990, you began working as an attorney?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, 1990, as we all know, saw the elections, the national elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time, did you get involved in the political process and were you elected to serve as a representative in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was elected member of parliament in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as an MP for the Serb Democratic Party without any political engagement, because at that time it was allowed for non-party candidates to be elected MPs provided that they signed a paper stating that they do not mind being candidates. So I was a freelancer but I agreed to be on the list and that is how I became a deputy in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to that time I understand you had been a member of the Communist Party but you left the party after the 14th Congress, which saw the dissolution of the party.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if I can touch briefly upon some of the positions you held after your election as a representative to the parliament, were you -- after the establishment of the governmental authorities of then the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and what became Republika Srpska, were you selected to serve as the Deputy Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And very quickly, how long did you serve as Deputy Prime Minister and what position did you hold, if any, thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I came to Pale on the 20th of May, I think, 1992. I spoke to the then Prime Minister of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and we agreed that he propose me as a candidate for a Deputy Prime Minister. This procedure took place in June when either the president, on behalf of the Assembly, or the Assembly carried through that appointment, my appointment to the post of Deputy Prime Minister. That government fell on the 24th of November, 1992 when Prime Minister Djeric resigned. We continued to serve until mid-January, roughly, 1993, when the new government took over, so that is as far as government service is concerned. In the second government, that Dr. Vladimir Lukic was Prime Minister of from January of 1993 onwards, I was advisor to the Prime Minister, I held that office, and that government was in place until August 1994, roughly. After that, I held no government positions. Parallel to being in government, I was an MP as well until, I think, the summer of 1994 when I was dismissed from parliament through a decision taken by the Serb Democratic Party. They decided to withdraw my mandate. This was not in accordance with the existing law, it was not in accordance with the new law, but that is how my activity in the National Assembly ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Just to clarify, I think this is the point with which the Court is very familiar, perhaps the record needs to be made clear but I'll seek some guidance from the Court on that. When you say you held no government positions after August of 1994, I understand that to mean that you held no position with the arm of the authorities known as the government in contrast to the arm of the authorities known as the Assembly or, for example, your president. Is that a distinction you were drawing in making that point, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. My position in government stopped when Professor Lukic's government was no longer in place. I, as an MP, continued to be active until I was relieved of my duties as MP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, can I draw your attention to the period of time after you began serving in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an SDS representative and the beginning of the outbreak of the conflict. During that time when you were serving as a member of parliament, did you work with members of the SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: While the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina was still one, a commission -- a constitutional commission was established, if that's the right name. But it was a commission that was supposed to work on amendments to the constitution and things like that. On behalf of the club of Serb deputies, Serb MPs, I was a member of that commission. The president of that commission was the president of the Assembly, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik. In terms of this agreement we had, I was the one who stood in for him most of the time at these sessions of the Constitutional Commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina when we were supposed to attend joint meetings in Belgrade and things like that. In fact, when the Constitutional Commission of Yugoslavia was still meeting when the representatives of Zagreb took part and the representatives of other republics, when he could not go due to his work in Sarajevo, then I would go. So of course there was this kind of cooperation. When we met up at Pale when war operations started, of course at first we were all there. All of us were cramped in this one building where there weren't proper facilities for work, but meetings took place every day and everybody was there. The leaders from the Presidency, Krajisnik as president of the Assembly, was here -- was there as a kind of host. Karadzic, Koljevic, and others came, one, two or three ministers when there were meetings there, practically every day. So those are the activities and cooperation I meant. This is this life we had together during this transition from peacetime to wartime. We did not know where our families were, we did not know where our bags were, you know, so we all lived together that way under these conditions in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Returning our attention momentarily to that period before the outbreak of the war, I'd like to play for you and for the Court a couple of intercepted telephone conversations during that period of time and seek your brief comment about those.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, Your Honour, if I can distribute the binders and obtain an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The four binders containing 114 tabs will be Prosecution Exhibit P583.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I wonder if I might just ask whether there is, or can, without too much work and time, be produced a hyperlinked version of the schedule of these 114 items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm clearly happy to oblige, as Mr. Stewart knows, if that's technically feasible. I wouldn't make that representation without checking with those who are better placed to answer that but I am happy to do so at the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, I'd ask you to first listen to a telephone conversation that took place on August 14th, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I believe there are two clips for those we'll play successively, Your Honour. One is relatively longer than the other, the first clip, and we'll play them in the succession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we find the transcripts somewhere in the binders?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. Tab 68, Your Honour. The first clip will begin at the beginning of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we stop the intercept, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I listen to the French channel, I receive a French translation, but the English is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I may ask the witness, Your Honour, Mr. Trbojevic was signalling, I think, that he was not getting it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not getting interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- interpretation. Well, you are supposed to get the original. Madam Usher, could you please check whether Mr. Trbojevic ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't. I can hear the interpretation into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then there must be a switch from channels because we received the original B/C/S whereas the witness, who was supposed to receive the B/C/S, did receive the English translation. Could we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The English booth hopes that it's going to be all right now. Can we start from the beginning, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we restart, please. Mr. Trbojevic, if you do not receive the B/C/S, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover]: Radovan Karadzic: Yes. Momcilo Krajisnik: Hello. Radovan Karadzic: Hi, how are you? Radovan Karadzic: I just got in. Momcilo Krajisnik: What are you doing? Radovan Karadzic: Well, I just got in, met some people and so on. Momcilo Krajisnik: Really? I've been here all day. Lots of things going on. Fuck it. Radovan Karadzic: So are you still at work? Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes. Radovan Karadzic: Really. It should be different. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes. Radovan Karadzic: You went to sleep early last night. Momcilo Krajisnik: There is no field here at all, I don't know how many pigs I've got or cows. Hello? Radovan Karadzic: Hello. Yes. Momcilo Krajisnik: I said I don't know how many cows or pigs I have. Radovan Karadzic: God is taking care of it. Momcilo Krajisnik: I hope so. What are you doing? Radovan Karadzic: You take care of this state and... Momcilo Krajisnik: I am but there are others too. Radovan Karadzic: Yes, yes. Momcilo Krajisnik: The Presidency was held today, you know. Some decisions were made. I don't know. I think we didn't understand something. I examined this platform a little. I think that that's not good. Radovan Karadzic: Do they say, ours ... Momcilo Krajisnik: I don't even know what they were doing, I think they ... they didn't get it right. Didn't understand it right. I have no idea what are we going to do. ... Believe me, it's all in the platform, Bosnia and Herzegovina is a sovereign state. I am afraid there will be a scandal and then there will be trouble. There's no Yugoslavia, this is two, three, five times worse than anything that was done until now. Radovan Karadzic: Well, then we will have a break-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Momcilo Krajisnik: Let me tell you, we shouldn't take part in the break-up, it is wrong... I think it would be good if we were to consult a bit with our people up there. I don't know why they did this. ... Radovan Karadzic: ... why is it ... Momcilo Krajisnik: I was with a guy who was present there. Radovan Karadzic: And what did he say? Momcilo Krajisnik: I think they didn't agree on what they want. Debate has finished, in Presidency, he thinks the debate hasn't finished. Radovan Karadzic: Well, the debate finished in the Presidency, now it is going to the Assembly, right? Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes, that's right, but I think that's not right, I'm afraid there might be problems in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Radovan Karadzic: They're going to the Constitutional Commission, right? Momcilo Krajisnik: No, it's going to the Assembly. ... Look, there are two problems, it was said that the platform goes to the Assembly but the problem is how it is treated from then on. ... You know, because that's what it is. They don't want it to have the constitutional character which it doesn't really have at all. ... So that there are two documents, one for creating a constitution. And today I got really angry. Believe me, I haven't been this angry in a long time. We have groups in the constitutional commission which have all kinds of meetings and international relations and so on, and I was supposed to be there and I said don't put me, put Mijanovic, Gaso, he is a professor. He's realistic, he is not such a Serb, but he will know what needs to be done. ... Milan should go with him and Krstan Malesevic on behalf of the SDP. ... One member of the government was proposed and one of the Presidency. Two government members and one Presidency member, each should be of a different nationality. And today, I get the document, it is unbelievable. ... Milan Trbojevic took part of it. I called then, Ranko was there for 15 minutes, Tmicic was, but he wasn't authorised, Mijanovic wasn't, Krstan wasn't. And I mean out of the Serbs who were there, Milan Trbojevic, he came to me and I said, please, we agreed about it nicely. ... There was some objection, somebody should summarise it. Later on it should be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. discussed. ... And they write, almost send to all the Constitutional Commission members and to other commissions that he is involved in it. Radovan Karadzic: You know what you'll do, let Milan Trbojevic write an official letter for you. Momcilo Krajisnik: Okay. I know what I did. Everything there. I say you have to report to your people, you're representing the interests of your people. He will really write it. It's a mistake of Cazim Sadikovic ... But it's impossible in this ... way. ... I said you will create a revolution. I don't think that something should be done now in favour of the Serbs, but you, people, cannot do things like that ... they will say that we betrayed. Radovan Karadzic: How did Trbojevic behave? Momcilo Krajisnik: How? Radovan Karadzic: He does not see any danger, right? Momcilo Krajisnik: That's a problem, I mean, it's really difficult when we -- when I have to say that, fuck Sim ... and Ranko, and I was there for 15 minutes, I was not authorised. Simovic sent Ranko, Ranko says ... he went away. So let them go ... Radovan Karadzic: Why don't you rub Simovic and Ranko a little bit? Momcilo Krajisnik: Well, I told them today, I was very angry. Do you realise, people ... can you understand what is going on? You don't have the right to convey this information. How can you do this? And then they said, well, you know, they said they got in -- well, I said, you can't explain it in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, the -- Your Honours, the second clip begins on page 5 toward --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do that, Mr. Tieger, could you have a look at the third page out of 7, semi-last box, where it says: "Karadzic Radovan: Nobody of ours took part in it, right?" I missed that in the transcript. There's no need to pay specifically attention to it but I just note that it's missing. Perhaps you can first ask the witness whether he heard that and then perhaps later on everyone can check. Mr. Trbojevic, we have a written transcript of this telephone conversation and just before the participation in the meeting was dealt with, in our transcript, it reads as follows, Mr. Krajisnik says: "One member of the government and one of the Presidency were suggested, two government members and one Presidency member, each should be of a different nationality. And I get the document today, it is incredible." And then in the transcript, it says, "Radovan Karadzic: Nobody of ours took part in it, right?" And then the next line is: "Krajisnik Momcilo: Milan Trbojevic took part in it. I called then, Ranko was there for 15 minutes..." That line where it reads, Radovan Karadzic to say, "Nobody of ours took part of it, right?" Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, before we -- well, let's play the second clip and then I'll ask some questions about the intercept generally. And again the continuation can be found beginning at page 5 toward the bottom in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover]: Momcilo Krajisnik: Listen, Radovan ... come on, please, I advise you to sit down ... I don't know really where since our club up there is working. Radovan Karadzic: If it doesn't work maybe my place would be better. Momcilo Krajisnik: Okay, we'll speak later, I'll call you at home ... all right. And let's try to organise it. Radovan Karadzic: I go home now, to get some rest, I hope Buha is not there, probably he isn't. Momcilo Krajisnik: I don't know. I will organise those you think I should, and then will let you know, right? Radovan Karadzic: Shall we call Milan, then? Momcilo Krajisnik: What? Radovan Karadzic: Shall we call Milan also? Momcilo Krajisnik: I don't think that's necessary. Radovan Karadzic: All right, we'll take Biljana and Nikola, you and me. Momcilo Krajisnik: Well, you can call him since he is important in that commission, you know. ... You -- why don't you see who needs to be there and then let's talk. Radovan Karadzic: I will. Momcilo Krajisnik: Okay. I will be home and then I will come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also here it seems that parts are missing, Mr. Tieger from our transcript. For example, I didn't -- I don't see -- for example, after it says "Shall we call Milan also," then it continues, "Well, you can call him since he is important in that commission, you know." Therefore, two lines are missing, both the line "I think it's not necessary," and "Okay, we can take Biljana, Nikola, you and me." Those are not appearing in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's correct, Your Honour, although I recall hearing that translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then -- well, then if that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If it's necessary to play it again to clarify the record, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to have this replayed again because I don't remember -- my attention was drawn to it since I didn't hear it when I was reading. Let's play the clip again, at least if that's possible without ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover]: Momcilo Krajisnik: Listen, Radovan ... Come on, please, I suggest that we sit down and talk. I don't know where since our club is working. Radovan Karadzic: It doesn't work, maybe my place would be best. Momcilo Krajisnik: All right, let's speak later, I'll call you at home. Try to organise it. Radovan Karadzic: I will go home now and take some rest, I hope Buha is not there, probably he isn't. Momcilo Krajisnik: I don't know. Why don't you gather who you think should be there and let me know, please. Radovan Karadzic: Shall we call Milan, then? Momcilo Krajisnik: What? Radovan Karadzic: Shall we call Milan? Momcilo Krajisnik: I don't think that's necessary. Radovan Karadzic: All right, then let's get Biljana, Nikola, you and me. Momcilo Krajisnik: Well, you can call him since he's important in that commission, you know. Radovan Karadzic: Yes. Momcilo Krajisnik: Why don't you see who needs to be there and then we will talk. Will you call me? Radovan Karadzic: I will. Momcilo Krajisnik: Will you be at home? Radovan Karadzic: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Trbojevic, did you recognise the voices of the speakers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that it is Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you're mentioned in that conversation, as we could hear, and also the Constitutional Commission. Can you provide us with some further understanding of what you understood that conversation to be about and what you recall taking place at that time and your involvement in it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to confess that I don't know what this was about. This was probably one of numerous meetings where issues were discussed, certain material arriving from all kinds of places. Based on this conversation, I can see that at the time, I gave an explanation and that it was agreed that all of these discussions had to be summarised and then further discussed, but I really couldn't tell you anything more about which parts of the Constitution, did this involve Constitution at all, I truly do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it, however, more broadly a reflection of your work in connection with the Constitutional Commission you mentioned to us earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Most likely. This was most likely part of my duties. Based on this conversation, I provided an explanation to the effect that this had not been completed and that opinions would be collected from all sides and that we would continue discussions. This probably had to do with some technical issues, positions, guidelines, how we ought to proceed, and so on. And it seems that it was expected that this would be further discussed and then decided upon later. Right now, I really couldn't tell you what this platform was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to next move on to the other conversation I spoke about, unless the Court had a question earlier, so I didn't want to cut off any question the Court might have, otherwise I'm about to move on to the next conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that can be found at tab 69, binder 2. [Intercept played].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover]: Milan Trbojevic: Good evening. Ljiljana Karadzic: Good evening. Milan Trbojevic: This is Milan Trbojevic. Ljiljana Karadzic: Oh, Milan, how are you? Milan Trbojevic: What's up? Ljiljana Karadzic: Well, I couldn't tell you myself - I spent the entire day in Pale and at work ... Milan Trbojevic: I was in Pale as well. Ljiljana Karadzic: Oh, really? ... Yes, I was in the former S house. Milan Trbojevic: Oh, I was in the municipality building. Ljiljana Karadzic: I was with these refugees. ... That's really horrible, when you arrive there and you see all the children. ... I really get depressed. Milan Trbojevic: Yes, it's quite unbelievable ... Ljiljana Karadzic: Horrible. I mean, it all seems to be so far away but it's actually very close. Milan Trbojevic: Yes, one wonders what our ethics is all about ... to live a civilian life here. Ljiljana Karadzic: Yes, that's terrible. ... Radovan is here, he arrived maybe 15 minutes ago. All right. Well, I'll let you talk to him. Say hi to everyone at home. Tell Rada that the colleague of mine took two days off so I didn't get to talk to her. ... Good-bye. Milan Trbojevic: Good evening, Radovan. Radovan Karadzic: Good evening. Milan Trbojevic: What are you doing? Radovan Karadzic: Well, I just arrived home. I'm resting. Milan Trbojevic: There must be a lot of work. Radovan Karadzic: No, no problems. Milan Trbojevic: How are you? Radovan Karadzic: I'm all right. What about you? Milan Trbojevic: I'm here at the office. Radovan Karadzic: Is it all right? Milan Trbojevic: I want to write something, it's all right, there is a lot of work. ... Look, I called you the other night, you remember ... when those people from the Jugopetrol came. Radovan Karadzic: Yes. Milan Trbojevic: And then the director of one private company, Strbac, asked me ... because he had some business contacts with them ... and he called me tonight ... after the conversation that you had with them. ... He has a feeling that his status in business relations with them is a bit less favourable. Radovan Karadzic: Less favourable? Milan Trbojevic: Yes. Radovan Karadzic: I didn't mention him at all. Milan Trbojevic: So he would like you, when you have a bit of time, for you to meet with him and me. Radovan Karadzic: Well, what does he have to do with that? Milan Trbojevic: Well, he bought some sort of derivative ... for hospitals and for ... I don't know who else. Radovan Karadzic: And he bought it in what capacity ... for his company? Milan Trbojevic: Yes. Radovan Karadzic: This is his private company. Milan Trbojevic: That's right. Radovan Karadzic: Well, let me tell you we have to put it all under one umbrella. I have to say that I had no idea that it was linked to him. ... We have to put it all under one umbrella because some of our institutions will be funded through that. ... Milan Trbojevic: Well, he would like us to meet with you. Radovan Karadzic: And what is he by profession? Milan Trbojevic: I don't know. He's been in commerce for years. Radovan Karadzic: I have no idea. I didn't mention him at all. I only said that we would soon establish an institution within our Assembly, you know, I couldn't -- I can't tell you about that on the phone but it would go through that so that we could finance our institutions from that. ... So it's not a problem. No, no, no, not a problem at all. I didn't even mention him. Milan Trbojevic: You certainly didn't. Radovan Karadzic: No, no, I wouldn't even remember him. Not at all. Certainly not. It's just that we have to stick to that now, we cannot be left without it. ... And we'll try to include him in our systems and that's all. Milan Trbojevic: So when are we going to talk about it? Radovan Karadzic: One of these days ... after the plebescite is over. Milan Trbojevic: All right. Radovan Karadzic: All right, deal. ... All right. Good-bye. Mr. Trbojevic, can you tell us, please, who is speaking and what the conversation is generally about.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Karadzic and myself. Obviously, I called. This conversation, in my deep conviction, is about trade and it has nothing to do with the activities of this Tribunal. Branko Strbac is a man who is deceased now, he died in the meantime. He was a person who was involved in trade and I met him in the corridors of courts as an accused person in different cases. We had known each other for years. He was involved in trade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate you were attempting to answer my question as best you could, but since you indicate the details of the conversation may not be of interest, I just want to ask you generally about the subject matter of attempting to finance institutions. Mr. Karadzic said, "We'll soon have to put everything in one basket because that's what some institutions -- or some institutions will be funded by that." Was there generally an effort at this time to find methods of funding for the SDS and the institutions of the SDS or institutions that would arise from ongoing efforts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You heard that he said during this telephone conversation, "I cannot tell you now but work is being done on it." I don't know what the SDS intended to do and how to secure its financing. I know specifically that I was asked to prepare and carry out the registration of a company which would actually be a stock company and it was the members of the SDS who would be the shareholders. You know what the procedure is like in a court of law in this respect, to fill out different forms, to have a meeting of shareholders, to have minutes about this, so -- and to submit all of that in court. So a company was set up, it was called Novi Privrednik. Now, what it did and how much of their revenue they gave to the SDS or whether they gave any of their revenues to the SDS is something that I don't know about because I was not a member of the board or anything in that company. I simply knew that it was there. After I took care of the registration, I had no further contact with this. And in this context, this Strbac asked me to bring him into touch with Karadzic because he wanted to be one of the trading partners of the said company. That was it. In that respect, I really have no further knowledge how long the company functioned, whether there are any written traces today in the court documents. I know that I sent the decision on the registration of this company by fax to Mr. Aleksimilovic [phoen] in Pale sometime in the beginning of 1992. Now, was the seat of the company later moved to Bijeljina or somewhere else is something that I really don't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, sir. I'd like to ask you to look at another document that involves the issue of funding, and that can be found at tab 114 in binder 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, to clarify, I'm only seeking the admission of the -- and only directing the witness's attention to the copy of the contract that is found in the article, and although the article is translated, it would be my intention to simply have the rest of the English translation essentially deleted, unless the Court feels it's necessary for context, and just focus on that contract itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, I recognise that the copy is a bit small, but I'm hoping you can make it out. It reflects a contract signed in Sarajevo on the 21st of November, 1991 by a Bauxite Milici represented by general manager Rajko Djukic and by the President of the SDS, Dr. Karadzic, for the supply of oil. And it indicates in part in Article 2 that Bauxite Milici hereby undertakes to pay to the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina as reimbursement for the said position and right the sum of 3 dinars per each litre of so acquired fuel. Mr. Trbojevic, do you know whether or not this contract represented another effort to find funding for the institutions of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I've never seen this contract and I don't know about this effort. I'm not familiar with this at all that the SDS gave this possibility to Milici to do so and how this was done. I really don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Djukic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Djukic was the director of this mine, Milici. Milici is a very small town. Most of the people are employed in the mine so the mine is everything, really. They built a pool for the community and many other things, and Milici lives on the profitability of the mine and the director of the mine is the main person in town. Now, was he the president of the executive committee of the Serb Democratic Party or something like that, at any rate, he was a high official of the SDS but I'm not sure whether I gave you his exact title. I met him a few times during the war and after the war. He's still the director. Even now, he's still the director of that mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I note also that in Article 1 of the contract, it indicates that the SDS undertakes to ensure for Bauxite the position of chief supplier of oil and oil derivatives for Bosnia-Herzegovina through Jugopetrol, and I recall that in the intercept we listened to involving the -- the conversation between you and Dr. Karadzic, you mentioned to him that -- you mentioned to him people from Jugopetrol, and I wondered if that refreshed your recollection at all about either general efforts by the SDS to work with Jugopetrol on the supply of oil to fund institutions or more specifically to Djukic's involvement in that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't know anything about any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned Jugopetrol because I probably heard it from Strbac, that the representatives of Jugopetrol were there and said that they would be selling oil through the SDS or somebody else but I really don't know Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be that in light of those answers -- it's not a big issue, but I confess I'm slightly puzzled by the suggestion to delete part of the English translation of this article. I suggest that either part of the article is deleted altogether from both the B/C/S and English as irrelevant or neither.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I understood that only the contract would be in evidence as published in a newspaper article, and that would be true both for the B/C/S and for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trbojevic. If I can turn your attention now to something you mentioned earlier, and that was your departure from Sarajevo and your arrival in Pale, which I think you indicated was around the middle moving into the latter part of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Around the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Mr. -- were you -- may I ask you this: Were you contacted by Mr. Djeric or anyone else before you left Sarajevo? In other words, while you were in Sarajevo, were you asked to come to Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And once you arrived in Pale, were you approached by Mr. Djeric or by someone else?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Branko Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Djeric's position at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: He was Prime Minister of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did he ask you to assume or undertake a certain position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: He said that he wanted me to be Deputy Prime Minister and that he would ask Karadzic and Krajisnik for their consent. And he asked for my consent in this respect, and I agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Djeric obtain consent from Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik for your selection and did you then assume the position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he talked to both of them or whether he talked to them at all, but I think that Karadzic signed the decision on my appointment. As far as I can remember, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me just mention, if I may, a portion of the -- of one of the conversations you had with the Office of the Prosecutor earlier and see if that refreshes your recollection about the conversation that you had with Mr. Djeric in that connection. That portion can be found in the interview of March -- the March interview at page 8. And at that time, Mr. Trbojevic, in discussing the conversation you had with Mr. Djeric when he asked you to assume the position of Deputy Prime Minister, you said, "Djeric told me that Karadzic and Krajisnik gave their consent." Does that refresh your recollection about that conversation and what you were told by Mr. Djeric at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot state with certainty even today whether he already had this consent for my appointment or whether he would get it subsequently. Believe me, it wasn't that important to me. So I didn't really think about it. I cannot say even today whether he said we had agreed that I should make this proposal to you or whether he said, "Do I have your consent to make this proposal?" I really cannot say. Both options are possible, but I really don't know now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the witness's microphone please be turned on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Mr. Trbojevic, you spent a lot of words in answering that question. You were confronted with the lines reading, "Djeric told me that Karadzic and Krajisnik gave their consent." Did he tell you? Did he say so to you? I'm not asking whether he got the consent, whether he got it prior, whether he got it later, whether he didn't get it at all. The question is just: Did Mr. Djeric tell you that he got the consent of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In all honesty, I cannot make any categorical statements to you now. What was important for me was that this consent was there and that I would stay there and do something. Now, whether he got the consent before talking to me or after that or whether it happened the same day or -- I really cannot ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, I precisely told you that I was not asking whether they got -- he got the consent but whether he told you that he had got it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He certainly said that, but I cannot tell you now whether he said that before talking to me or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So he told you that he got the consent of Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. -- Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik. Now, part of your previous answer was, you said, "What was important for me was that this consent was there and that I would stay there and do something." Would that mean that, without this consent, you were not confident that you could stay and do something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, you recall the date of your formal appointment and perhaps it's not necessary to take time to show an exhibit that indicates your formal appointment as Deputy Prime Minister on the 8th of June, but let me ask you if you began to serve informally as Deputy Prime Minister before that point.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I started immediately on an informal basis, immediately after that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you give us some idea of your --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Or actually, I started working formally but without a formal appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you give us some ideas of your duties and responsibilities as Deputy Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, as for any precise formulations of the authority vested in the Deputy Prime Minister, there weren't any. I don't know when the law on government and the law on ministries was passed, where this is specified, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm -- let me -- we may well move into that, and I apologise for an ambiguous question. What I had in mind, actually, was what kind of work did you undertake as Deputy Prime Minister? What did you do, who did you meet with, what sorts of activities were you engaged in after you assumed the position of Deputy Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Practically -- at that time, cabinet meetings were held practically every day, so I immediately had to face many problems that the government was dealing with. All sorts of problems, all sorts of types of problems with different contents. So there were consultations every day with the ministers, with certain working groups that were preparing some regulations, with practical problems due to the relocation of schools, universities, then the need to establish a service that would control the border, like a customs service. Then there were attempts made to establish contact with the government of Serbia and the government of Yugoslavia because companies from our territory had parts of their companies in their territory. Now, what would happen to them? There were efforts made for companies that were in our territory to go on working, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you attend sessions of the Assembly of the Serbian People?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you -- you mentioned earlier you served on the Constitutional Commission in the joint Assembly, did you continue to work on constitutional issues and did you serve on any related commission in the -- associated with the Bosnian Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you attend meetings in connection with that commission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What, exactly, was that commission attempting to do, briefly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, there are written documents. I think that twice, we adopted amendments to the Constitution. We discussed that, I mean these materials, and I think that all of that was adopted. Everything that was done was ultimately included in the text of the Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there a chairperson of that commission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik was chairman as president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And who else was a member of the commission or attended the meetings of the commission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Karadzic attended some of the sessions. I know that Mr. Vojo Maksimovic was there. I know that Professor - the name escapes me now, and he was mentioned in that first telephone conversation - Gaso Mijanovic. Then Dr. Radomir Lukic. As for MPs, I cannot remember now who could have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall if Dr. Koljevic attended meetings of the commission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know now. Possibly, but believe me, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And again, let me direct your attention to a portion of your previous discussion, one of your previous discussions with the Office of the Prosecutor that can be found at page 17 of the March transcript. You were discussing the commission and you indicated that, "... as a member of the commission, we were often having discussion on amendments of the Constitution and the presiding, the chairperson, Mr. Krajisnik. Very often also Mr. Karadzic was present." Then the conversation continues, and you say, "As I said, I recall talking to, or discussing constitutional amendments on several occasions, that Krajisnik was the chairperson most of the times, that Karadzic was also present, Koljevic was also very often present ..." Is that consistent with your recollection, sir, of those meetings of the Constitutional Commission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you, Mr. Koljevic is someone who was a friend of my parents, so every time he and I met, there was a lot of pleasant sentiments involved and I was always very happy to meet him, to sit next to him. Frequently, we would attend the same meetings, cabinet meetings and so on. Now, as to whether he sat next to me in certain meetings of the Constitutional Commission, I couldn't say, but it is probable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, could I ask you to carefully listen to the question and to focus on answering that. The question was not whether you were sitting next to Mr. Koljevic. That's a matter you introduced yourself. The question was whether it's your recollection, as you stated before, that Koljevic was also very often present in this committee. So that's the question. What you did, as a matter of fact, is explaining on your mutual background why it would be so nice to sit next to him, and then you answered the question you put yourself, whether you were sitting next to him. The question was whether Mr. Koljevic was present often.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is it is very likely; however, I cannot claim whether that was once, twice, or on more occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So there is no doubt, as I understand you, that he was at least one time present, and whether it was more times, you do not recollect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. We will adjourn until 11.00, not a quarter past 11.00 but 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In respect of -- Mr. Tieger, will we hear any further intercepts, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I don't have to make any observation in that respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two quick matters before I do. First, I would note that we were able to provide the Defence with the requested hyperlink table during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A CD. And second, perhaps I could, at this time, tender at least for identification the transcripts of the interviews we've been referring to and it may be best, although I leave that to the Registry, to have them marked as tab 115 rather than making a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just express my thanks for the prompt provision for the hyperlinked CD, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any further observation in respect of the transcript of the interviews? Then you said you have tab 115, that is -- yes, the same four binders then. Yes, these are two interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, one dated 23 March 2004 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Judges have them, so there's no need to again distribute ... Madam Registrar, a problem is they don't fit in the binder any more. Madam Registrar has a better suggestion.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The interview dated 23 March 2004 will be P583A, and the interview 4 May 2004 will be P583B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, before the recess, you had mentioned, among other things, the meetings that were taking place in Pale and had referred, I believe, to cramped quarters or people being cramped and perhaps you can describe the location and physical layout of the places where the members of the Bosnian Serb authorities with whom you were meeting were located.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In the very beginning, there was a building. When one leaves Pale on the way to Jahorina, it was on the right-hand side. It was a longish building, a motel of the company whose seat was in Kikinda as a result of which the motel itself was called Kikinda Motel. There, in a room, in a small room, individual meetings took place attended by several persons. That room, as far as I could see, was also used by Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Krajisnik. In addition to that, there was another larger room where a dozen or so people could fit. So sometimes meetings attended by ten or so people would take place. That lasted for a short period of time. After that, we transferred to the Hotel Bistrica in Jahorina, which is where the seat of the cabinet was. In that building, there was sufficient room; there were several rooms which could accommodate minister cabinets and there was also a cafeteria there. There was usually quite a crowd there. Then in another building called the Panorama Hotel, there were offices where Mr. Krajisnik, Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Karadzic, the secretary of the Assembly were. And in addition, there was a small conference room there as well. Occasionally, we would hold meetings in that conference room, such as the meetings of the Constitutional Commission and so on. That's what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how far apart was the Hotel Bistrica than the Panorama Hotel and Kikinda Motel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Panorama is on the road going from Pale to Sarajevo. That's where it is located, some 500 to 600 meters away. I never really analysed this but definitely not more than a kilometre. As for the distance between Kikinda and the Jahorina mount, that is probably some 10 kilometres away. The Hotel Bistrica is 10 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you say, "We transferred to the Hotel Bistrica in Jahorina," who were you referring to as "we"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to Branko Djeric, myself, the secretary of the government cabinet, Mr. Lokic, several ministers. Velibor Ostojic was there, Ljubomir Zukovic, Bogdan Subotic, Petar Markovic, the minister of finance. I don't know if I omitted some names. There were probably others but I cannot remember them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately when that move took place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say with precision. Probably in the course of June 1992. I'm not sure about that, but I think in early summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, during this period of time, Mr. Trbojevic, did you have an opportunity to see the various figures you've mentioned interact with one another at meetings and -- both formal and informal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you are referring to specifically. We were all there in one building. I'm referring to the cabinet members now. We met almost daily in various government meetings. And in preparation for meetings, we naturally had contacts with each other. Contacts at various levels; sometimes we would meet at lunch, sometimes we would have coffee together, and sometimes we discussed such issues as who was going to what location, what problems we had so that we could attempt to solve them together. Everybody communicated with everybody else, if that's what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned many figures in the various organs of the Bosnian Serb authorities. Can you tell the Court who the most powerful and most important or most influential person or persons were among the Bosnian Serb leaders?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: The question is quite unspecific. You want me to give you my assessment or my opinion about certain things that may or may not be in my memory any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask the question this way then: In 1992, who, among the people you mentioned, or anyone else that you haven't mentioned, exercised power over the policies and organs of the Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You see, the principles were set forth in the Constitution that there were three branches of government: Judicial, executive, and legislative, and that they were all separate from each other. It is my assertion that all of us took the position that this is how it ought to be, and this is what needs to be ensured. I claim that all of us in the government wanted for the rule of law to prevail and in a situation where the country was in chaos, where there was lack of communication lines and so on, it was very difficult to ensure that. Therefore, the Assembly was an organ that met frequently in those war times. This organ did take position concerning the most important issues, including the negotiations. The Assembly consisted mostly of the MPs from the SDS, which means that the political authority was in the hands of that party. There were several MPs who were not members of the SDS. I, myself, was on the SDS ticket but was not in their organs. So us who were in that situation took on the role of some sort of the opposition, which was quite impotent under the circumstances. Now, as to the military organs, which represented the power, the force, and if you're asking me about the authority of the police, which originally was intended to ensure internal law and order, these are all relative issues. As for the government, we had the minister of defence there, who, at least from the outside, didn't seem to have a lot of authority. Now, as to his relations with the General Staff and the Supreme Command, this is something that we, in the government, knew nothing about. There was also minister of police, who had a certain amount of raw force at his disposal, and either by way of regulations or by way of pragmatic situation, he was in contact with other members of the cabinet but again represented the force that was not under the control of the government. Now, what could the various inspection organs do? Not much. The parties didn't have a chance to file complaints and so on because this was wartime. Therefore, the government turned into a firefighting service, so to speak. The Assembly was a forum where political life of Republika Srpska unfolded. And as for what Krajisnik and Karadzic did in order to formulate the position of the SDS, I really couldn't say anything about that because I was not a member of the party and I did not personally attend those meetings. To what extent negotiations with international figures affected the formulation of their official position, and to what extent that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. official position again was under the influence of the people from Belgrade, I couldn't say anything about that. What I can say is that the government of Republika Srpska had no cooperation with the government of Yugoslavia or Serbia. They did not see the government of Republika Srpska as a government. But the governors of central banks from one place and the other would meet, you know, when there were issues to be discussed. There were also some contacts concerning commerce.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me stop you at this point and try to focus us a bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask a question, please. I'd like to know how many members there were in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember correctly, there were 82 MPs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you said, Witness, that they were not all members of the SDS. How many members were not members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact percentage, but less than 10. Less than 10 MPs were not members of the SDS. If I'm not mistaken, there were 7 of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those who were not members of the SDS, were they able to air their views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. We were critical. We expressed our proposals, which are reflected in the minutes; however, that did not affect the decision making, the voting on various issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did they have a total freedom of expression, or if they were to air their views freely, did this trigger an aggressive response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say that there were aggressive reactions. They were individual expressions that were, perhaps, improper but I don't think there were any aggressive reactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no penalties imposed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Later on, they started expelling certain individuals from the Assembly, but in this other period that we are discussing now, there were no sanctions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, was there a person or persons who were -- who was or were regarded as the leader or leaders of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: That, again, is a matter of personal view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Mr. Trbojevic, based on your position as deputy minister, your many contacts with the various members of the Bosnian Serb authorities, your discussions with them, with the leader or leaders of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I will tell you that the broadest view was that Karadzic was the leader. In Serbian language, we have an expression, a term, Vozd, which is an old Slavonic term for a leader. So this term Vozd was popular among the people because it carries certain weight. In Banja Luka, we had a chairman of the local SDS, Dr. - his name escapes me now - who liked to refer to himself as the Krajina Vozd, the Krajina leader, which, naturally, had no practical significance. But if you ask me, based on what I heard and what I saw, who was the leader among the leading figures in Republika Srpska, I think that that term could only be applied to Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was there any person with whom Dr. Karadzic was particularly close?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: It is my impression that Dr. Karadzic had the closest, friendliest relations with Dr. Koljevic. As for the efforts aimed at creating Republika Srpska, conducting all the negotiations, all the affairs, contacts, and relations with the Assembly, then if we are referring to that, then naturally, he cooperated most frequently with Mr. Krajisnik. I have to say that in their conduct and in their contacts - and here I'm referring to Krajisnik and Karadzic - Krajisnik manifested in all situations that Karadzic was the president, that he was the supreme leader, and that he had the last say. He never allowed himself to oppose Karadzic in front of other people, even when he did not share his views. I think that he did his best in order to express any different views to Karadzic when they were alone rather than in front of the Assembly. At least, this is how I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Would you say, based on your observations of the two of them, that they were -- that they had a close relationship and worked closely together?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that they cooperated very closely. Now, as to whether they were truly close, personally, I couldn't say. I don't think that they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I direct your attention, Mr. Trbojevic, to a passage during your second interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, in May, and I'm referring to page 33 of that interview in the English translation, in which you said in the middle portion of the page, it appears after the first time your name is indicated in the left, "They were very close to each other. I don't know what it was like before, but I know since that trial and after that they were in detention, and since then, they became like two bodies and one soul, and in that kind of community, it was my impression that Krajisnik was like the major part of their basis." What did you mean when you said, "They were like two bodies in one soul"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I used a figure of speech there. The two of them had a certain position, as far as we could tell. They had the same political position and there was no divergence there between the two of them. As for the political orientation and political activities and how they ought to be guided, it is my belief that the two of them had an absolutely identical position regarding that. And as far as that is concerned, this is what I meant when I said that there were two bodies and one soul.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also said that it was your impression that, "Krajisnik was like the major part of their basis." Can you tell us what you meant by that, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I put it that way exactly, the way it's written there, and I don't know actually what is written there, but this is what I meant ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, if you feel more confident that we check that on the tape, we'll do that. If there's really -- if you have any hesitation as to this is what you said, we can check that on the basis of the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not hesitating. I'm not hesitating, there is no need. I can explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, perhaps you literally then confront Mr. Trbojevic with the parts and tell him that this is a quote from the translation made from the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps that clarification suggested by the Court is indeed quite helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was reading to you from the transcript from the tape during which questions were posed to you in English by the OTP representative and you answered in B/C/S and it was translated by the interpreter. Again, I was reading from the transcript of the interview, at page 33 of the May interview, where you said, "Since then, they became like two bodies and one soul, and in that kind of community ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, my attention is drawn to it. We'd like the witness to be confronted with the whole of this paragraph and perhaps I'll read it to you slowly, Mr. Trbojevic. The question put to you by Mr. Margetts was: "Your observations at the time was that Krajisnik was more organised and an effective decision maker." That is what is at least said to be a question, whether it was a question is another matter. Then you responded: "Yes, I was convinced in that. They were very close to each other. I don't know what was like before, but I know since that trial and after that they were in detention, and since then they became like two bodies and one soul, and in that kind of community, it was my impression that Krajisnik was, like, the major part of their basis. I had opportunity to see, like, when Krajisnik would have some remark, Karadzic would change his attitude. I didn't see the vice versa. It was nothing ... It was reference to nothing important, but that is something that makes ... that shows the relation between people." That is recorded as your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I'm saying today as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Between the two of them, Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, were you able to observe who was the more organised of the two, who was the more effective of the two?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They are two different words, two different concepts and, therefore, two different questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I think -- well, let's -- put the question as you want it but not two different questions in one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you able to observe who was the more organised of the two, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I said during that interview, and it's not hard for me to confirm it once again: Mr. Karadzic seemed like a totally disorganised person; a person who does not take notes, a person who does not collect documents, a person who has no system in his work. At least, that's what I saw and that's my assessment. Mr. Krajisnik, though, is a person who writes down what he agreed upon, with who, what he planned, what he wants to resolve. So he shows that there is something systematic in his attitude towards the work that he does. That is why I had the impression, that is my deep conviction, that Mr. Krajisnik, compared to Mr. Karadzic, is far more organised, systematic, more reliable if you agree on something with him, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Based on your observations of the two of them as you described them, including the opportunity to see Mr. Krajisnik making a remark and Mr. Karadzic changing his attitude, including Mr. Krajisnik's organisational qualities in comparison to Mr. Karadzic, who appeared to you, between the two of them, to be the leader, if one could be said to be the leader rather than the other?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: There was no dilemma there. Karadzic was the supreme chieftain, if I can put it that way. If there was anybody who was in charge, it was Radovan Karadzic. There was not the least bit of a dilemma there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So can you explain, then, exactly what you meant when you said -- and I'm referring now to page 22 and 23: "My personal impression is and many other people would agree with my feelings that, in the unity of the two of them, Krajisnik was much better organised, much more efficient, and if anybody was a leader, it was Krajisnik who was leading Karadzic."

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: That is my assessment of their private relationship, if I can put it that way. The relationship in which the two of them are not the president of the republic and the president of the Assembly, they are people who socialise, they both have their own jobs, and in this relationship, in my deep conviction, Krajisnik was more superior because he was more systematic, as I said. He would stand by what he would promise. He would prepare what needed to be prepared. And that would, indeed, be prepared most probably. Whereas that was not the case with Karadzic. If you agreed on something with Karadzic, that meant that you'd have to remind him of it, that you'd have to see whether he actually did initiate something, whether it had gotten to a point where it was supposed to be, and so on and so forth. What I meant was the relationship between the two of them. It is my deep conviction that Krajisnik was more thorough, more focused, and vis-a-vis the outside world, Karadzic was someone who had a charisma, a charm, the ability to manipulate masses, if you will, now that we're talking about my impressions, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then, about their relationship with others within the Bosnian Serb authorities. What was the extent of the authority that Mr. Karadzic -- or Dr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik had in connection with the deputies of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can't really say. There was a sentence, for instance: "He is Karadzic's man." And then there would be another sentence: "He is Krajisnik's man." Now, who belonged to who is something people could not know, or rather, I did not have the possibility to know because I was not within this internal system of the Serb Democratic Party. You see, that pertained to members of the SDS, members of municipal committees who'd go to Pale, who'd talk to both of them on most occasions; sometimes separately, sometimes together. Now, who trusted one of them more and the other one less and who cooperated with one of them more and with the other one less is something that I cannot really tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At page 8 of the May interview, Mr. Trbojevic, you said -- and again this appears in the first -- after the first specific reference where your initials appear, that would be the second full paragraph, second sentence: "It is a fact that ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'd like to confront the witness with the -- with his statement then in the context. I'll read it to you. You were asked about in 90 per cent effective control by Krajisnik, or at least the vast majority of the deputies. Your answer was: "I don't know how did we understand each other, then. It is a fact that Krajisnik and Karadzic had something what was like very close to the absolute authority. There were discussions at the sessions, at the Assembly, and there were different attitudes and there were confrontations, but when it came like to final attitudes and getting the decisions and I know that there wasn't a single time like that, for example, what two of them would suggest, that Assembly would reject. There was characteristical example, when there was a discussion about signing the peace treaty that Karadzic signed." And then you further explain how that happened in the Assembly, whether they would -- it says "verify," but I take it that it is "ratify," but at least what was signed on the ship. That's what Mr. Tieger is confronting you with now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I explained it there what I meant by that. So what are you interested in now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps first of all, we are interested in whether you stand by what you said at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that is exactly the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'll just draw your attention to it that it's not exactly, to say it very gentle, that you did not phrase your position exactly the same way earlier during your testimony in this courtroom. But perhaps that saves a lot of time. I'd like to confront you with another part of that same statement. We find that on page 10. You were talking about Djeric rejecting something, and then Mr. Margetts said did Djeric, did he reject the fact that his government could not set policy or did he reject the policies that were set by others for the government to implement, or both? Your answer was, "Most likely, it would be both." The next question was: "And who set those policies?" Your answer: "As I ... As I said before, it was by Krajisnik and by Karadzic and that went to the party and went through the Assembly and through the other organs." Then Mr. Margetts said: "So, you are describing the situation where Krajisnik and Karadzic effectively had absolute authority or power in a practical sense over the Presidency, Assembly, and the party." You responded by, "Yes." Do you still stand by the answers you gave in May 2004?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
