utterances.text: If I could turn your attention to the first interview, at page 30. The question was asked at the top of the page after a discussion about who -- first there had been a discussion about who Subotic, Mandic and Stanisic reported to or didn't report to, and then you were asked by

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: "So operationally you think the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Ministry of Defence, and to some extent Ministry of Justice was being run by Karadzic and Krajisnik?" And you responded: "Yes, the police and the army definitely. And when justice is concerned, Karadzic was in capacity of his authority, the function he had was making decision of appointment. So, practically, justice was also in his hands." Do you stand by that answer as well, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: There's not the slightest bit of dilemma that Karadzic appointed people to positions in the judiciary. It depended on him who would become a judge or prosecutor or who would not. The fact remains that this did go to the Assembly and that the Assembly would confirm it, but people were actually appointed by Karadzic signing this appointment, especially as far as judges were concerned. Now, as far as authority was concerned, Mr. Margetts formulated the question as best suits him. I would not claim that I was a witness of this absolute power and its exercise. I explained to him that all talks about peace negotiations and all decisions that were reached by the Assembly were indeed at the Assembly. Before that, they were probably discussed by the organs of the SDS. I explained that this could not move if this agreed upon by Karadzic or Karadzic and Krajisnik, and perhaps somebody else too, maybe Mrs. Plavsic and maybe Mr. Koljevic, but I did not say the words "absolute power" as Mr. Margetts did in his question. Now, how the decision was made as for the functioning of the military, the army, and then part of the police that, in cases of mobilisation, would become part of the army, that is something that the minister of defence would have to know too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I please stop you. I'm a bit confused as to what question you're actually answering to at this moment because in the last question and what was put to you, I did not hear anything about absolute power, whereas it seems that you're commenting on words used by Mr. Margetts during the interview about absolute power. It might be that you are still responding to the previous question, or questions, especially where the words were used "absolute authority." Is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I heard, the Prosecutor read Mr. Margetts's question and he used the words "absolute power" in terms of the functioning of the judiciary, the police, and the army. That was the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The words used were -- let me just check that. My recollection is that he used for Mr. Karadzic the words that "justice was in the hands of ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would be happy to read the question and answer again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The question I previously read to you, and the answer, Mr. Trbojevic, was as follows: "Question: So operationally, you think the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Ministry of Defence, and to some extent the Ministry of Justice was being run by Karadzic and Krajisnik." Your answer was: "Yes, the police and the army definitely. And when justice is concerned, Karadzic was in capacity of his authority, the function he had was making decision of appointment. So, practically, the justice was also in his hands." Was that an accurate response to the question, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you mentioned Mrs. Plavsic in one of your responses and you had mentioned Mr. Koljevic earlier. Let me ask you first if there was a difference in the authority of Dr. Karadzic and Krajisnik on the one hand and the authority of Mrs. Plavsic and anyone else with whom she might be associated on the other; and if so, how great was that difference?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, again, that's a question of my assessment as a spectator. I know that we were preparing a law on the implementation of the Constitution, and what we envisaged there was that before it became possible to elect a president of the republic, there would be a Presidency and that it would consist of two members. The people who were meant were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mrs. Plavsic and Dr. Koljevic. They were the people who were elected to the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war. So formally, it was considered that they should be the ones who would be the top instance in Republika Srpska. In practice, this was changed. The law was changed, Karadzic was elected, et cetera, et cetera. And now that you're asking me about authority, it is my deep conviction, most sincerely, that Karadzic had its own authority that was high above everybody else, Krajisnik's was below his, and Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic were leaders of a second or third degree, if I can put it that way. This was the usual assessment made by people who had the opportunity of seeing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are just going to change area a little bit and move to a slightly different subject. I would like to know whether you felt that the Assembly was playing an effective role.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was not a decisive role. The Assembly was the venue where practically all topics were brought up and all dilemmas were aired, all topics that were discussed. But I think the decisions were made under a great deal of pressure from the Serb Democratic Party, and of course Krajisnik and Karadzic were its proponents by the very nature of things. So it can be said that the Assembly was the body that carried out its legislative powers in accordance with the policy charted by the Serb Democratic Party. This was publicly formulated, if I can put it that way. This was the situation as it was and it was opened -- it was obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For those who are not familiar with the Dutch testing system, this kind of sirens, that's always at exactly 12.00 on the first Monday of the month, so no one has to be worried about it. It will take approximately one minute, but I think we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am referring to what you said in your statement, your first statement, on page 20 and 23, you say as follows: [In English] Krajisnik knew very well that his delegates will vote for an issue that he was interested in. Krajisnik was formally with the presiding the chairperson of the Assembly. He was the one who was evaluating the feelings and the climate among the delegates. He was the one who would recess or stop the session if he had a feeling that the climate is not right for the decision to be made the way he felt they should be... [Interpretation] I would like to know what you mean by this, sir. Could you please comment on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I wanted to say. I described that example involving the verification of an agreement that Karadzic had signed. We gathered in the hotel called Jahorina at Pale, or whatever the hotel was called, and this was the meeting of the MP club and we had to discuss whether the Assembly would verify or ratify that agreement the following day. One of the MPs asked that the agreement be copied and distributed so that we could see what is it that Karadzic had signed, and then Krajisnik said, "No need to do that. The key points had been taken out of the text and distributed, which is enough in order to inform everybody about the contents." Because naturally, these issues had been discussed earlier. This was a practical approach. So the session of the Assembly started, we entered the room and debated for two days and two nights, and if you hear some dissonant voices to the effect that it ought to be verified, Karadzic, who had already signed that, could not very well come out and say, "I made a mistake." And when it became a little bit suspicious as to how many MPs actually asked that it be verified, Krajisnik said, "Let us stop with the session and once again meet in the caucus." This was already 2.00 a.m. We met in another room and Krajisnik said if we were to postpone this, if we do not actually want to adopt a decision, let us make copies, distribute them to the MPs and postpone this and then meet at a later time, and then postpone it again and then meet again, and then one realised that this was all actually a game. First they didn't want to make copies, but rather, wanted to adopt the decision, and then afterwards, they said, "Okay. Let's make the copies and then postpone the session and decide later on." So this was all just a situation to which I reacted perhaps improperly and left the session, but this was just an example showing that things could be manipulated if the discussion took a wrong course and it could be terminated and then debated further in the club, and then rescheduled the session. I don't think that this is unusual, that this is an unusual practice in various collective bodies, but this is what we discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, you mentioned Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic as elected representatives to the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina who later became part of the Presidency of Republika Srpska. When you first arrived in Pale in mid or latter part of May, who were the members of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say that now with any precision because I know that there was a law on implementing the Constitution setting forth that the two of them were the Presidency, or members of the Presidency. Later on, that was amended and it was stated that the Presidency would have three members, and then Karadzic was elected to that three-member Presidency as a member. And now as to whether they formulated that he should be the third member of the Presidency or he was appointed to that function by the Assembly, I really don't remember that. But initially, in the beginning, it was the two of them who constituted the Presidency. I don't remember exactly now because the law was later amended, but I think that it must have been the two of them. I know that we said that the two of them were the only ones who were, in fact, elected in the general elections and that that ought to be preserved, and this pertained to Koljevic and Plavcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And subsequent to that three-person Presidency, was the Presidency, the membership of the Presidency expanded further in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know when that decision was taken. I remember I discussed once with Branko Djeric, when he came in the morning to the government meetings, he said that he was in the building where Karadzic, Krajisnik, Plavsic, and Koljevic had offices, and since all of them were presidents of certain bodies, they were frequently to as presidents, president of this and president of this. Now, as to when the decision was taken to transform this into a three-member Presidency, I really couldn't tell you. The decision must exist somewhere. I personally did not take part in preparing that document and do not remember it specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And my question didn't pertain to the three-person Presidency which you had already mentioned but to whether or not that three-person Presidency was then expanded.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I meant, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just -- Mr. Trbojevic, you give long answers, not very much focusing on the question. The question was clearly whether the three-person Presidency expanded later in 1992. You said, "I do not know when that decision was taken." First of all, we'd like to hear from you whether you know about a decision. Could you -- do you remember a decision which expanded the three-person Presidency into a more than three-person Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm doing my best to explain the actual situation. I said that I did not personally participate in the adoption of that decision, in formulating its text, therefore, I don't know when it was signed and adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are constantly answering a question which was not specifically put to you, certainly not by me. That is when the decision was taken. I first want to establish that such a decision was taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that that decision was adopted. I particularly didn't know when it was adopted. I heard from Branko Djeric that it was going to the -- that he was going to the Presidency sessions, and based on that decision, he was supposed to be a member of that expanded Presidency. This is how indirectly I heard about this term "expanded Presidency."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you were told by Mr. Djeric that he was a member of an expanded Presidency; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said he was going to attend the Presidency sessions, that he had to attend them, that he wasn't pleased about that because these meetings always took place at night, late in the day, and so on. I knew that he attended those meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know about anyone else, apart from the three members that was Karadzic, Plavsic, and Koljevic, apart from Mr. Djeric, to be present during this meeting, any other person which, in addition to the persons I mentioned, would attend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who attended the sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know whether only the four persons mentioned did attend these sessions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When the Presidency was expanded, who were the members, irrespective of who may have attended the meeting, of the expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how come I know that, but I think that the expanded Presidency consisted of Karadzic, Krajisnik, Koljevic, Plavsic, and Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you recall the date on which that expansion -- the approximate date on which that expansion of the Presidency occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I draw your attention to page 29 of the second interview in which you discuss some extracts from the Constitution. You explain in that answer some of the things you had been mentioning here, mentioning that the function, on the seventh line of your last answer on that page, that "... the function of the president will be conducted by Presidency of, like which will have three members." Then as your answer continues, you say, "And the other law is like some kind of amendment to law from June 1992. They are now bringing like a new organ. They change ... they change the Presidency and they say that during the, like, war conditions that Presidency will be made wider with President of the national Assembly and the president of the government. I think that is now the most important decision." Does that refresh your recollection, Mr. Trbojevic, about when the Presidency was expanded to five members?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts probably showed these regulations to me. We went over them and this is how I came to read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer correctly, and please correct me if I'm wrong, you knew from Mr. Djeric that the Presidency had been expanded but when you were answering the question in court, you didn't recall the date but based on your review of the laws, you -- during the time of the interview, you understood that the expansion took place in June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: If that's what is stated in the text of that decision, the text of that enactment, then that must be how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you or Mr. Djeric have a view about why he was included in the expanded Presidency in addition to Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I truly never analysed that, never thought about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, have you expressed the view before that Mr. Djeric was included in the Presidency so that when Mr. Krajisnik was added to the Presidency, people wouldn't comment on that in particular?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm actually referring to page 31 of your interview in May, where you were asked why you thought the five-member Presidency was formed. That's the last question and answer on that page. You say: "I don't know how that happened. I have ... I was very sure that even this three-member Presidency was functioning only based on authority of Radovan Karadzic and authority of Momcilo Krajisnik, who was not member of the Presidency at that time, although ... although formerly he did not have those authorisations as the President of the Assembly. That's why I think that there was a possibility to include him into this organ, which would give him some legitimacy as a part of the supreme body ... supreme organ of power, because the president of a republic, by its function, is closer to executive powers than legislative powers. And I believe that Djeric was included into that Presidency, probably in order to avoid people thinking why Krajisnik was there too. Because it ... or it would be logical that the president of government would enter that kind of organ, because he is executive organ and he should have the greatest number of information at his disposal. But knowing the relation between them, he was not included into the Presidency in order to be given status of, like, being part of that highest level of power. I believe it was only for a reason that ... when Krajisnik entered there as a representative of legislative power, so this way they also say that Djeric as executive power could do it, would enter, too." Does that refresh your recollection, Mr. Trbojevic, about such a view and is that an accurate reflection of your understanding of why the Presidency was expanded in the manner it was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: This was obviously one of the thoughts I had. I have no ability of proving that this is actually how it was. I have no evidence to prove that. This view is valid, that there is no room for a president of the Assembly in that kind of an organ, whereas it is logical to have the Prime Minister a member of that organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, may I ask you one question in that respect. This analysis or these thoughts, you just explained to us that they were rather theoretical about logic, what was logical, what was not logical. Are there any circumstances which supported your view, were there anything apart from your own thoughts that supported your analysis of Mr. Djeric becoming part of the Presidency just in order to make people not think the wrong things, as far as I understood you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said just a moment ago that I have no way of proving this. This is just one of my thoughts. Perhaps it was developed as a result of my discussion with Djeric who was not happy about becoming a member of the Presidency and having to attend the meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's exactly why I put this question to you because "prove" does not mean -- if I have no proof of something - and I'm now talking about normal life and not about being in a courtroom - if I have no proof of something, then sometimes I, nevertheless, may have some knowledge of circumstances which would support an idea, although not prove an idea. So what I'm asking you is whether you had any circumstances in mind or knowledge of any circumstances that would support your analysis of why Mr. Djeric was included in the expansion of the Presidency, although perhaps not proving it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing specific to offer you. The fact is that they had offices in the same building, Krajisnik, Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, they had offices next to each other. They could have discussed issues whenever they wanted. The mere creation of that organ seemed unnecessary. Therefore, what I said is just one of the comments concerning that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say, "The mere creation of that organ seemed unnecessary" Because, as far as I understand, you said they were so close in terms of their offices, that they would not need an organ, well, to have their conversations. Let me put it to you in a different way: If you have this kind of cooperation or conversations, et cetera, that it would be proper to formalise them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for the witness. In your evidence on page 29, you are referring to the expansion of the Presidency, you stated: "[In English] I think that this is the most important decision." [Interpretation] What have you got in mind with this? Why was this the most important decision? Do you think that it was an important decision because it was a change in the structure which was most unconstitutional or is it because of the consequences of that decision; and if any, what were those consequences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Initially, it seemed to me that it was unnecessary. We were all in the same building, next to each other. We would see each other several times a day. And now all of a sudden, here we are creating an organ which is supposed to formalise our meetings, and we all have the duties that we had; therefore, I thought that that was superfluous, unnecessary. In addition to that, it was not in accordance with the Constitution, so one wondered why would we violate constitutional provisions even though it was wartime. The consequences themselves, what decisions were adopted by that organ, I have to tell you that I did not give it much thought. I did not analyse whether that would bring about any changes in the policy pursued and in the work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just repeat my question. Why have you stated, "I think that this is the most important decision"? Why have you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which section this referred to, this sentence that I said. Really, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about the point in time in which you say, "They changed the Presidency [In English] and they say that during the war, the Presidency will be made wider with president of the national Assembly and the president of the national -- of the government. I think that it is now the most important decision." [Interpretation] I just would like to know why you said that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I did not say that. I think that must be a mistake in the text because during that interview I said that that Presidency, in real terms, did not have any consequences of its establishment. As for what was actually happening, and I must say that I did not see any of that, and therefore, I simply cannot agree with what it says there, unless this was taken out of context, unless it referred to something else. As for the decision to establish the Presidency, I certainly could not have said that that was the most important decision because, actually, it just remained on paper, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we have to have a break now. In view of the last answer of the witness where he says, there must have been a mistake in the transcript or in the translation, I would like you to do two things: First of all, to provide the witness whenever possible, not through direct contact, but with the relevant page of the B/C/S, if there is a B/C/S version of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Trbojevic, you will be presented with a B/C/S copy of the page you are just confronted with and we would then like to hear from you whether you still take the position that it has been misinterpreted. If so, we'll check on the basis of the tapes whether this is supported by the recording, and we could do that by having the original tapes being replayed. We will adjourn until five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I do understand that there was some hesitation to give the witness just the one page. The only thing the Chamber had in mind was to verify to what extent the complaint about translation or recording was correct or not, and the witness has been confronted with two or three lines, and certainly you would need the context because he -- I think he put that in a certain context which, as far as the Chamber is concerned, does not necessarily lead to giving him the full copy of all of it but at the same time, we're not opposed to it either, but perhaps -- I didn't hear from the Defence any observation in this respect, but I'd rather limit it to the relevant portion, even if you'd say that the line of questioning, if that would be two or three or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. four pages, that's fine as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I understand, Your Honour, and I agree and I thought that is what the Court was indicating but because there was at least some room for ambiguity, I thought it was safer to do otherwise. I have those portions here if the Court would wish to do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not necessarily now. I think the witness has answered the question. Part of his answer was that in the translation his words were not reflected as he has said them. He could read that page over during this afternoon and this evening and then report to us tomorrow and see whether there's any need to further clarify the matter by hearing the audiotapes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, in connection with your responses about the expanded Presidency, I believe you mentioned something about seeing it in some respects as superfluous or unnecessary and you mentioned the regular meetings that were taking place even before the expanded Presidency was formed. Let me direct your attention, if I may, to a portion of your second interview, found at page 32 at the bottom. We were discussing the same issue. And the question refers you to the appointment of Krajisnik and Djeric to the expanded Presidency. And you said -- the question was: "You said that the appointment of Krajisnik to the expanded Presidency meant that he formerly held a position with an executive function; is that correct?" I want to pause for a moment and hopefully give the interpreters time to locate it in the B/C/S transcript. Then you said: "Yes it is. I yesterday said that his status and before entering this wider Presidency, it was the same. And functioning of Krajisnik and Karadzic even before entering Presidency was of the same level, of the same power and of the same base." The rest of your answer doesn't directly address that issue, although it touches upon it, so I'll stop there. Was -- did that answer given in the May interview, Mr. Trbojevic, capture the sense in which you were indicating your feeling that the formal expansion of the Presidency was superfluous or unnecessary?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about the institution of Crisis Staffs. First of all, were you familiar with the existence of Crisis Staffs in the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in different forms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And to what extent did you understand that the Crisis Staffs held power in the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that the government, as an institution, that it did not have any direct insight into the work of these Crisis Staffs. Actually, hardly any. I had the opportunity of talking to people in Sokolac, and on one occasion, I toured the municipalities in Herzegovina. I visited Nevesinje, Gacko, Bileca, and Trebinje, and let me say that this is some personal experience that I had in this regard: We saw a situation there, that the war was already over in a particular town, or perhaps some war operations were over, a number of people left as refugees, another group of people came to town as refugees again, so these Crisis Staffs actually had to deal with the issue of where to put up the people who came, how to feed them, how to have at least part of the economy functioning, how to ensure that the school operates; all the regular needs of a town or a community that were suspended due to the war. The government would be asked to send fuel by way of assistance for vehicles, and food for hospitals, and now the question is how the administrative authorities functioned. Of course, there is the problem of response to call-up by conscripts and also the problem of the return of conscripts to town. Can both happen? Then there is the major problem of safety and security because soldiers return from the front with weapons and the question was how to ensure the safety, the vital safety of citizens, because soldiers who are armed and outside their units are dangerous anywhere. So that was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn our attention for a moment away from the -- whatever the specific problems that may have been faced or addressed by Crisis Staffs to a more basic question of whether or not the Crisis Staffs were the power in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as the Crisis Staffs are concerned, there was some kind of instruction that was sent out in terms of the establishment of Crisis Staffs. Crisis Staffs were envisaged as organs that were supposed to make it possible to have the legal authorities function. So the Crisis Staff was supposed to be led by the president of the municipality, and the president of the executive board of the municipality was supposed to be on the Crisis Staff. So those were supposed to be the most responsible people who would be dealing with the most pressing problems, and the assemblymen of the municipality were supposed to try to get the Assembly together as soon as possible so that the system would start operating, if I can put it that way. So if you look at the concrete situation, as for the resolving of concrete problems, well, yes, the Crisis Staff did have the authority to decide on matters that actually fell under the jurisdiction of the Assembly. Also, to see how different positions would be allocated within the municipality, but actually, they were not supposed to be any kind of form of government, they were supposed to be there until the regular authorities would start functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And during the time the Crisis Staffs existed, was power in the municipalities vested in them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that they were the mainstays of practical authority until the municipal Assemblies could start meeting again. No one ever thought that it should be envisaged nor was it envisaged that Crisis Staffs should have any kind of authority in terms of using the military or the police. In many Crisis Staffs, there were members of military commands and police structures only for the reasons that I mentioned a while ago; namely, to coordinate the sending of conscripts to the front line, then that the unit should make it possible to have conscripts sent back home, and also that these conscripts should not move around, armed and posing a danger to the population. Then the police would have to adapt their activities to the military units because part of police also had some of their activities under the military units involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And from whom -- from which bodies or which individuals did the Crisis Staffs take direction? To whom were they answerable?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I've said that the government sent this instruction on the establishment of Crisis Staffs, if I remember correctly, sometime in the month of April, before I came to Pale. It is a fact, though, that we as members of the government, had poor communication links with the municipalities, partly due to the war operations, partly due to the lack of communications equipment. Afterwards, the regulations changed. A decision was passed on the establishment of War Presidencies, then War Commissioner's offices. I don't know which one came first, but if I'm not mistaken, these decisions were taken by the Presidency. The first one was poorly formulated. The legislative and executive were brought together within the Crisis Staffs - that was rectified later - but the concept was supposed to be as follows. I mean, the concept that the government insisted on was the one I explained to you just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were the Crisis Staffs party organs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they weren't party organs. I think that the party was supposed to send people to the Crisis Staffs. Now, the president of the municipality would be a person from the party, then the president of the Executive Board would be a person from the party as well. So there was no doubt that the Serb Democratic Party had a dominant influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In your second interview, at page 69 of the English translation, you say at the very bottom of that page: "So practically the Crisis Staff was a branch of the party." And I'll read the question that preceded that and the full answer. The question was: "So, they had power in the municipalities and you said they were answerable to Karadzic and Krajisnik. So, what was your observation in respect of ability of Karadzic and Krajisnik to effect action in municipalities?" You said: "So, they had like absolute connections both, with deputies and with the party in the field. Like, in the Crisis Staff, you had people who were part of the party, part of the ... were also deputies and were also members of the board of the party. So practically, the Crisis Staff was a branch of the party." Was that a correct answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I said just now too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned the police in connection with your answer concerning Crisis Staffs and I'd like to ask you some questions about the Ministry of the Interior, if I may. If I can turn your attention to a portion of tab 106, the 22nd session of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's the beginning of binder 4, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me first turn your attention to an excerpt from page 48 of that Assembly session in the English translation, which I believe can be found at approximately page 49 in the B/C/S translation -- page 47 of the B/C/S translation, at the top of the page. What you said then was: "However, when it comes to the police, I have already said this at one meeting, I don't know if it was the Assembly, but I think that the law on internal affairs has set the relation between the minister for internal affairs and the Prime Minister in the wrong way, the same way that the law on army excluded the minister for defence from the relations with the state ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we have not found it yet. You said page 47 of the B/C/S translation and page, was it 48 in the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that would be the fourth paragraph; the second paragraph from the bottom. It's the paragraph that begins, "We have tried to make schedules ..." and then continues. I began reading at the second sentence of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "However, when to comes to the police, I have already said this at one meeting, I don't know if it was the Assembly, but I think that the law on internal affairs has set the relation between the minister for internal affairs and the Prime Minister in the wrong way, the same way that the law on army excluded the minister for defence from the relations with the state Presidency." And I pause, Your Honour, we might want to check the translation on that. "The same is in the law on internal affairs, the minister of internal affairs is directed at the state Presidency, not at the Prime Minister." Mr. Trbojevic, did that express your concern about who the minister of interior was reporting to and who the minister of interior was not reporting to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before I continue, let me ask you -- direct your attention to remarks by Mr. Djeric at the same Assembly session, found at page 17 of the English translation in approximately the middle. And at page 12, I believe, of the B/C/S translation, toward the top. Mr. Djeric speaking and saying: "Further, if the Prime Minister has free hands to make quick changes and if someone else takes the right to insist on some ministers, then, gentlemen, he needs to take responsibility for their work. So far, not a single member of the state leadership has done that, but they always say it is the government's responsibility, the responsibility of the Prime Minister, and so on. For example, when it comes to the justice system, when it comes to the minister of justice, the minister of internal affairs, they are not even in the government, they never come to the government sessions, only to the president of the Republic or the president of the Assembly. Neither of them ever stood up in front of the people or on television and said, 'We are responsible for their work,' which would release the Prime Minister from the responsibility. That would be a fair thing to do." Now, can you tell us, Mr. Trbojevic, what you and Mr. Djeric were referring to specifically in those passages, what concern you were expressing.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to admit that I haven't found this section where Mr. Djeric said what you read out just now. But I know that I said that some things were happening that did not have a proper logic and that should not be happening that way. At one point I mentioned that the minister of defence said to us that he reported to the General Staff in Belgrade, and in the part that you are reading now, it says that the function of the minister of the interior is linked to the Presidency of the Republic. And in this way, it was basically taken out of the government. So we tried to make a proper schedule this way. Part of the police is involved in military functions, but then another part of the police has to keep the law and order, but there was no one to discuss this with or agree upon with because they did not talk to the Prime Minister, they did not inform the Prime Minister about their activities, so the government remained totally uninformed about this sector of its activity which was supposed to fall under their ambit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, I want to give you an opportunity to find the excerpt of Mr. Djeric's speech that I read earlier, and in the English translation it appears shortly before Mr. Mandic speaks. And Mr. Mandic begins to speak at the top of page 13 and I directed your attention to approximately the middle of page 12 in the B/C/S version. My question is, in addition to complaining that the minister of interior and minister of justice were not reporting to the government or him as the Prime Minister, was Mr. Djeric also complaining that the minister of justice and the minister of interior reported to Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if -- as the Trial Chamber sometimes might asks, I wonder if Mr. Tieger might just give me a phrase so I can find it by computer search.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "For example, when it comes to the justice system, when it comes to the ministry of justice, the minister of internal affairs ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just a phrase would do. "When it comes to," is a phrase, right? Thank you. Got it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, have you been able to find the portion of Mr. Djeric's remarks where he addresses concerns about the minister of justice and minister of interior and to whom they are reporting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: It starts on page 11 here. On the same page, just below the mid-page, he speaks about the problems of the Ministry of the Interior, Ministry of Justice, and says this is when the problems started, this is when the government encountered problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the part where we find that would be on page 12, not on page 11, approximately the last 10 to 12 lines of the first linea on page 12.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you are interested in this portion where the Prime Minister says that the government has to be -- has to have carte blanche for any changes. If somebody else wants to have ministers at their disposal, then they have to be accountable or held accountable for their work. This was the discussion after a failed attempt of Mr. Djeric to carry out a partial reconstruction of the government and to replace Ministers Stanisic and Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You say, "If somebody else or anybody else wants to have ministers at their disposal, then they have to be accountable." Who was he referring to in using the term, somebody else who wanted to have the ministers at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Based on my conversations with Djeric, I know that in his attempt to reconstruct the government and to replace Ministers Stanisic and Mandic, based on what he told me, he had had discussions with Karadzic and Krajisnik regarding that and did not receive their approval, their consent. This was before the session and probably pertains to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, could you clarify something for me, please? You said, or you hinted that neither the interior minister nor the minister of justice were reporting to the Prime Minister and that the people they reported to be tended, in fact, to be Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik. If they had reported to the Prime Minister, what could the Prime Minister have done more than what he was actually doing? What difference would that have made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prime Minister wanted the cabinet members and the government to function in such a way that the government would be informed about what the ministers were doing. He wanted the government to be the one to inform the Assembly and the president of the Republic about their activities and their work. It was not logical for the minister of police and minister of defence to cooperate with the Presidency without informing the government about that and about the content of that cooperation. As for the minister of justice, I don't know what kind of cooperation he could have provided except in the matter regarding appointment of prosecutors and judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm still asking you the same question: What changes would have been made, or what would have been different in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is hard to say what would have happened if this situation in the government was different. I suppose that the insisting on -- ensuring law and order and so on ought to have been enforced to a greater degree. I suppose that the situation regarding the government's duties with respect to the army would have been better had we known, had we been properly informed on all aspects. This is especially true of the justice organs had they known what everybody else was doing. Now as to what they would have done specifically, it's hard for me to say that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you present at any meeting when Mr. Djeric attempted to -- spoke to Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic about his effort to eliminate or remove Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Mandic from the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps only once. Perhaps I was present only once. I mostly received information from Mr. Djeric, but I think that on one occasion we talked about that. I was present and I'm sure that Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic were present as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the occasion that you were present, did Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik both reject Mr. Djeric's proposal to remove Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Mandic from government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't say that this is how it ended, that it ended with them saying, "This is out of the question and we will not discuss it any more." However, they were against it. Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic sided with Mr. Djeric. Later on, the Assembly was held in Banja Luka where this was supposed to be formally pushed through and at that time, Djeric told us that he had talked to them and was told that this was out of the question. Then he attempted to reconstruct the government partially, I think without Stanisic, but with Mandic present as minister without portfolio. We voted on that and voted -- the vote was in favour of that, and this issue remained until Djeric resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I could go on, Your Honour, but that's my last question at this moment on that subject and I would be moving on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll finish it because then it's a quarter to 2.00. That was your last question or there was one more question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, that was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I misunderstood you. Mr. Stewart, you are on your feet just to hear me say that we are adjourned until tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm on my feet out of respect for the Trial Chamber because I believe that Your Honours are about to be on your feet to leave the court. No more and no less than that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will first announce that we will adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, but in courtroom II, not in this same courtroom. Mr. Trbojevic, I would like to instruct you that you should speak with no one about the testimony you have been giving until now and you are still about to give in the coming days. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 5th day of April, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.
